utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My apologies for the delay in the Chamber coming in today. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it wasn't actually me who pressed the button. It seemed to have come on voluntarily; I don't know if it's a sign from God or someone else. But may I deal initially, please, with two or three preliminary matters. One I hope Your Honours should have received at lunch-time today a list of witnesses that we are hoping not to call and it should start with a gentleman called Degin [phoen]. Can I just indicate that my learned friends have just had a chance of seeing it themselves. I clearly have got to discuss that with them, whether there are any issues that may require our clarification, but that is our intended position at this time. In respect of the 89(F) witnesses, I certainly did mention it on Thursday. We have looked at the witnesses completely afresh, and we take the view that perhaps Your Honour is right. It might be better if we just call the witnesses as they stand at this time. We are dealing with Velepromet witnesses, none of those should be 89(F), Ovcara witnesses, and then we go into the military witnesses. I would not expect any application for 89(F) for Velepromet or Ovcara witnesses, but in respect of the military it depends on the nature of the cross-examination, whether there would be any duplication and whether there is any need to, as it were, repeat or duplicate that evidence, and I suspect that can be clarified fairly soon after we embark on that group of witnesses themselves. We have in this trial been taking two or three witnesses a week. We anticipate that there are approximately 30 witnesses to be called at this time, and therefore we will fall within the time-scale of the end of April for concluding our case. Those are the estimates that we have worked out. In respect of the agreed facts, we have actually agreed a large number of facts but they need to be fine-tuned. I've spoken with the Defence today about one matter, and I hope that that can be resolved. It relates to the number of people found at the grave, the removal of one word and perhaps replacement by another, namely "patients" with "persons," because perhaps the Court might want to determine who are patients and who are not. And I think that is a perfectly reasonable objection by the Defence and we will change it to "persons." And in relation to other matters, I believe that we are fairly close to concluding that. There is one matter, however, that I would wish some assistance from the Court. I mean it not in any discourteous way at all. The Defence have agreed or admitted that there has been a conflict, and there is a conflict. Whether it be internal or international, I don't think there is any dispute about that at all. And I had the feeling, if I may use that phrase, that there was the possibility that a constitution expert might be called by the Defence, that that was going to be become an issue. Now, if that is the case, I would like to think that that matter would be stated now in open court. I understand clearly that the Court must determine certain elements in relation to jurisdiction. But if there is any constitutional argument, in my submission it should have been stated in the Defence briefs. It would be an issue that we would wish to consider. At this time, we take the view that there is evidence from Okun which covers that topic. But I think in fairness to the Prosecution, we would submit that if there is going to be a constitutional expert called here that we should have notice of the problem, if it be a problem, or, should I say, of the issue that requires clarification. And we submit that should have been pleaded at the very outset, if that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Mr. Vasic, are you able to assist on that last point?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to all. Thank you very much, Your Honour. I believe I am able to assist on this last point. If the Defence's understanding of what the indictment states is correct, and this is what we are acting upon in this trial, the mention there is of the existence of a conflict. I don't think the issue of international conflict is raised in the indictment. We would indeed be challenging that. Otherwise, however, there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you can take it that the Chamber sees no hint of international armed conflict in the indictment. That might help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, it does, Your Honour. Thank you very much. We believe this to be an internal conflict, and the question raised by my learned friend as we believe will not be raised in such a manner that we would be compelled to call a constitutional expert as part of our Defence case. There may be a number of other categories that might be challenged throughout this trial, such as the constitutional role of the JNA, or tasks and obligations stemming from the constitution itself, or the constitutional role of the Presidency and the federal secretary for All People's Defence. As for the nature of the conflict, I think the situation is rather clear, and I don't think there will be any problems in that respect, as my learned friend has pointed out. As for the agreed facts, the Defence would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to the fact that last week we agreed on more than half of those, which is a great deal more than the expectations had been for this. And after my learned friend put forward his own position, there was just one fact that the Defence teams found themselves unable to agree, at least not in the form proposed by the OTP. As my learned friend has just stated, we are well on the way to agreeing on that point, too, and we hope to be able to submit a motion to the Trial Chamber as soon as possible on all the agreed facts agreed by the parties through our mutual cooperation. There is another matter that I wish to raise. I'm talking about the obligation that we took upon ourselves. We promised the Trial Chamber that we would consider the positions of the Defence teams in relation to the statements that we were given by our learned friend pursuant to Rule 66(A)(ii) in relation to witnesses who have already been heard or part heard before this Trial Chamber. The Defence has done its best to, first of all, act in the best possible interests of our clients, but also to contribute to expediting the proceedings. We cut down our proposals only to those cases that in the view of the Defence are necessary in order to still be in compliance with Article 21 of the Statute. The Defence believes that in view of the fact that witnesses Bosanac and Njavro are anyway expected to return to the Tribunal to give further testimony that this opportunity should be used to allow the Defence to cross-examine these witnesses - I'm referring here to the Mrksic and Radic Defence teams - to cross-examine them on the points raised by the new documents that we have in the meantime received. As for Mr. Sljivancanin's Defence, they did not even begin to cross-examine Mr. Njavro. Therefore, we believe that the Defence team should be allowed, once Ms. Bosanac is here, to cross-examine her on facts related to documents received later on. As for Mr. Njavro, the Mrksic and Radic Defence teams, we believe, should be allowed to cross-examine him on matters related to these new documents. Mr. Sljivancanin's Defence is yet to cross-examine this particular witness anyway. The Defence has two further proposals. For this purpose, it might be a good idea to go into private session, since I am about to mention two witnesses who are using a pseudonym and who at least in part testified in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I'm not sure if I've answered all the questions that were asked. I certainly hope that I have, because at this point I have nothing further to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I just be clear, Mr. Vasic. Are you proposing that in addition to Mrs. Bosanac and Dr. Njavro that the witnesses P-013 and P-021 be recalled? Is that what you are proposing?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Vasic. I take it you were speaking for all three Defences, were you? Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I do have one or two small issues, so to speak, to raise before this Chamber. I will try to be very brief. On the 15th of November the Defence moved that a document be marked for identification. The number of this document was 67. The reason it was marked for identification is the English translation was missing at the time. In the meantime, we have been able to obtain an English translation; it's already introduced into the system. As these conditions have been met, we would like to tender document 67 into evidence as a full-fledged exhibit now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received, Mr. Borovic. I was just casting my eye about for objections. There seemed to be none. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The other more important matter that I wish to raise, and I -- that we believe the Chamber should deal with is a problem faced by the Defence in relation to a witness statement, number 5022. This is a crucial witness to Miroslav Radic's defence. Even the status of this particular witness might change if the Defence is able to find their way around, in a manner of speaking, while cross-examining this witness. But in view of the fact that as early as the 13th of October, 2005 we asked the OTP to serve on us the statement of this witness, I regret to say we only received it by mid-January 2006. I think the OTP is very fair, and I think we have a very successful cooperation, but as they know themselves based on the indictment that this witness is essential to us. I wonder why only one day has been put aside for the cross-examination. We had received on CD both the B/C/S and the English translation of this statement. Pursuant to Rule 66(A)(ii) and Article 21 of the Statute, I believe the OTP should do their best to serve on the accused a transcript in a language he understands. The interpretation is possible that the CD should do, and the accused and his Defence team should somehow be able to work with that. However, there are over 11 hours of recorded conversation on the CD, which means five times 11 hours by the Defence and the accused in order to prepare properly for cross-examining this material witness. To keep it brief, since this seems to be technically possible, can the Chamber please urge the OTP to serve a transcript of Witness P-022 to both the Defence team and the accused himself. That is all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Nothing? Thank you, very much, Mr. Lukic. If the court registry officer would receive that Exhibit MFI 67. It's been done, so it is now Exhibit 67. Thank you. Mr. Moore. First, perhaps the last point raised by Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we go into private session, please, in relation to this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are in a position to proceed. The witness is outside. To assist the Court, I will be taking the unusual step of leading this witness in relation to certain medical problems which he received as a result of matters in 1991, 1992. And I want to deal with that first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. If the witness could be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would you please stand and take the card in your hand that is offered to you now? If you would read aloud the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could we have your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: My name is Josip Covic. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And what age are you now, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I am 67. I will be 68 in two months' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, in a few moments I will ask you about matters concerning Vukovar in 1991. But I want to deal, please, with the very end of your ordeal when you were in a camp and then subsequently released to Zagreb. Can we just deal with that very shortly? When you returned to Zagreb, what sort of medical condition did you have at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: When I returned to Zagreb my health issues were multifold. I had a severe pneumonia, broken jaws, as well as my nose. I had concussions on my brain as well as injuries to my spine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in hospital when you returned to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: After having returned to Zagreb it lasted throughout 1992. I spent that year in several hospitals. If necessary, I can be more specific as to their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we go into private session in relation to certain confidential matters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, may we deal please in very brief form, what was your job before 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Before 1991 I worked with Elektroprivreda as one of the managing sales staff. The company dealt with the distribution of electricity. That was my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And could you be described as being politically active before 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was active. Politically I used to be a member of the League of Communists until the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal then, please, with May 1991? I think it's right to say that there was an incident at Borovo Selo. I think the specific date was the 2nd of May. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it very well. There were some employees from Borovo Selo, and we heard the shooting inside the company compound, and the people from Borovo Selo told us about what it looked like there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you take any part in any organisation of what I will neutrally call the defence of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. It was at that time that the potential defence started being organised in case there would be an attack against the city. And I was called in to help, since I used to be a reserve officer of the JNA. My military term was as one of the students at the reserve officers' school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what was your role at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Having in mind my age, and my health status, because in 1992 I underwent a difficult lung operation, my role was rather advisory, if I may say so. When the attack on Vukovar occurred, my primary role was to procure food for the defenders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think it's right to say that your son was also involved. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was involved. I offered advice in terms of how to defend mainly in the sense of their own protection, to increase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us that you were an officer in the JNA. If I take the time-scale from May 1991 until November 1991, can you tell the Court or assist the Court in describing the type of weapons that the people defending Vukovar had?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, the defenders had hunting rifles given by the hunters and the odd M-48. I don't know how they managed to purchase them. I guess from various sources, but I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What about what I will call heavy weapons? Did you see or can you describe to the Court the heavy weapons that the Croat defenders had?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning they had no heavy weapons. Later they did, but they were very few pieces. There were several artillery pieces, guns, and some of the weapons came from Borovo. There used to be a factory or rather a department in the factory which dealt with machinery and they used to produce something for our defenders. And the defenders kept saying that those pieces served them well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How did the number of those pieces compare with the heavy weapons and number of the opposing JNA army?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: A comparison of heavy weaponry owned by the defence and the actual shelling by the JNA against Vukovar, well, it is very difficult to compare. The difference was enormous. When the attack began, shells were raining. There were a thousand shells a day at least that fell on the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether those shells that you have described were targeted only on military targets or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: No, not the military targets. There were no military targets, there were only the defence lines of the local population and the defenders who came to our assistance. They shelled the entire city irrespective of where the defenders were located. That is why lots of civilians were injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And finally this: What about uniforms for the Croatian defenders? Can you tell us the extent of the uniforms that they had?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: There were very few uniforms, perhaps an occasional part of a uniform. The only people who had uniforms were the police who were also counted amongst the defenders, and they came to our assistance from Zadar. They were uniformed as policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us deal with what I will call the coordination of the Vukovar defence. Where was that coordinated?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Coordination of defence, well, the defence commanders would send out people, individuals to the lines of defence and they provided advice as to how to defend. Since I was in the role I described, I forwarded such advice to the defenders and I told them to dig deeper trenches so they could be better protected when defending.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And where was the ZNG headquarters located, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: The headquarters of the defence of Vukovar was across the street from the municipal building. Before the war that building housed the recruitment office. There was a nuclear shelter in the building and that's where the defence headquarters were situated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask you now, please, about airplanes. Did you see any airplanes being used to attack Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was in our part of the town, Vukovar -- that is the outskirts of Vukovar towards Bogdanovci. We were shelled and bombed. I saw our defenders bring down a couple of planes. They had hand-held rocket launchers. After that the sorties were reduced, but the howitzer and gun shelling increased as well as the use of mortars. That is, they used all artillery weapons they had available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you ever see any JNA or ships on the Danube being used?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I personally did not see that. But the people who were near the Danube told me that, the people who were close to the high school. That is at the foot of the hill and from that point they could see Backa, and behind Vukovarska Ada they saw some ships in Dunavac, and those ships were opening fire at Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal with the forces who were active against the Vukovar enclave? Did you see any paramilitary forces being used against you at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see paramilitary forces because I was never at the front line or at the first line of defence. The basic function of people like myself and the parents was to provide food for the defenders; that's what we did. It was very difficult to do, because we were out of electricity and water and food, and it was very difficult for us to secure food for them. But that was our principal function. And what we heard was what we were told by the defenders. They would tell us how the day went and such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We have heard evidence that loudspeakers were used against the Vukovar defenders. Were you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware, and I heard of it. A loudspeaker was used and one could hear Seselj's voice. Seselj, the Chetnik, we called him, just Seselj, according to his last name. He moved about and the defenders saw them, and they told us we recognised him by his voice. He moved between the barracks to the part of the town called Petrova Gora, and he was calling out to Ustashas to surrender. And we learned from him that Blago Zadro was killed and he said we would be killed the same as Blago Zadro was unless we surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you remember any other things the person that you believed to be Seselj was saying?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: The only thing I know about him is that when he was in the area he would spend his nights in the house of a local person by the name of Vojnovic. He was the managing director of Tehnostan before the war, and he stayed at his house. That's the only thing we know, and we were told that by the defenders.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters would kindly ask Mr. Moore to move the microphone closer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is that closer to me or closer to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: To speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did Your Honour happen to hear a reference from the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, he's asking you to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I hope they can hear me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal now, please, with a different topic? I want to deal with what is being called the fall of Vukovar. Is it right that at one time you were in the Sajmiste area?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, please stop touching the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at Sajmiste all the time. As I mentioned before, my basic task was to provide food for the defenders and to take back the wounded to the hospital. That was the most difficult thing to do, because we had to go to the lines and return the wounded back to the hospital. Perhaps on the 2nd or the 3rd of November we withdrew towards the stadium. The part between Sajmiste and the stadium is called Rupa. That's where we withdrew to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us then deal, if we may, to what could be called the day that Vukovar fell. We knew that to be the 18th of November. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's usually taken to be the 18th, the 18th is usually taken to be the day of Vukovar's fall. But that was the day when most of Vukovar fell, as it were. The day of the final fall was the 19th, in fact, because back on the 18th Borovo Naselje had not yet fallen, and this was part of Vukovar. So if we're talking about the town in its entirety, the city in its entirety, I would say the 19th. However, our authorities decided that the 18th should be marked as the day when Vukovar fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And where did you go to when Vukovar fell?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: When Vukovar fell, we spent that last night on the premises of my company which happens to be near the hospital, the distance being about 50 metres. That was where we spent the night between the 18th and the 19th, right there inside the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it's right that eventually you went to the hospital. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the morning of the 19th we went to the hospital. A number of persons did, and I was among them. We wanted all the civilians who were in my company, and there many of those, not just our employees, but people from the surrounding areas, to be taken to the hospital compound in the hope that once we were there we would be the first to be exchanged and sent back to free Croatian territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you describe to the Court what it was like at the hospital that day when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: When we first arrived at the hospital we asked for the hospital director, Ms. Bosanac, to inform us about the general situation. She told us that this particular district had already fallen in its entirety and that the aggressors were encircling the hospital. She told us to all come to the hospital, if we could. I personally went several times back and forth between the hospital and my company's premises in order to talk all the civilians, as there were women and children there too, into coming with me to the hospital. To this very day I'm still glad I managed to persuade them, and we finally reached the hospital compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be able to estimate how many people were in the hospital compound on the afternoon of the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: The 19th, I'm talking about the 19th, because we had spent the previous night in the company, and it was early on the 19th that we went to the hospital. I would say there were about 2.000 or 3.000 of them there. That's my take on it. However, I am certain that people who went to some of the upper floors of the hospital would say, would put the estimate at more like 5.000, but it's very difficult to say. It's a difficult call to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you remember the arrival of what I will call JNA/TO forces at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: It was not before that afternoon or evening. It was beginning to get dark and there were two hospital gates, as it were, one facing Ivo Lola Ribar Street, the other facing Bozidar Adzija Street. We saw some local people there who called themselves the TO. Across the way from the building, I believe the psychiatric ward was there, we saw several soldiers there and later on we also saw a number of JNA officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to remember what the TO were saying at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: It must have been about 8.00 or 9.00 p.m., night-time, that we observed, not I personally, someone from reception asked to speak to me, and this friend of mine said he thought I should stay within the hospital compound. I was still standing in the corridor, but he then told me that there were officer there speaking to some persons wearing white coats. He said he didn't know if these were the Red Cross people or the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not wish to interrupt the witness. However, I would ask my learned friend to try not to lead the witness this much. I missed something on page 29, line 1. There was a reference to him being at Sajmiste, that was a leading question. Further, page 27, line 5, another leading question. Further, page 27, line 13, another leading question. All of these questions I believe to be leading. Since the witness is being examined in chief, I believe the questions should be phrased in a different manner. If I am right, I would ask the Trial Chamber to please warn the OTP about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I realise that a number of these questions are merely guiding the witness to particular subject matter, but it's also fair to say that you are probably approaching a fairly sensitive area and caution is called for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we just deal with the time that you were at the Vukovar Hospital, Mr. Covic. Did you see any TO or JNA on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I see objections being raised by my learned friends. I submit that is not a leading question at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, it's not leading. It's directing to a subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, can you answer that question for us. Did you see any JNA or TO soldiers at the Vukovar Hospital or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw two TO members. As we were being boarded on to those trucks in which we were driven to Velepromet, I saw that group of officers standing at about 30 or 40 metres from me. It was night-time but you could clearly see by their uniforms that those were JNA officers. Standing with them, as we later learned, was someone from the UN, persons who at the time I believed to be the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you recognise any members of the TO who were in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I recognised those two at the main gate facing Ivo Lola Ribar Street. One of them was called Ziko. That's what we called him. The real name was Zivojin Jergic. He worked in my company, and this Zivko, Zivojin Jergic, was approached by a local man from Vukovar hoping that he would save us, since we were mates from work. He went there to speak to him and he asked to see me personally, another friend, Pero Nacuk [phoen] and his son who at the time was aged 18. He said we were fervent Ustashas and he wanted to kill us. That was one of the two TO men. The other was -- the other side of the gate when we were leaving in those lorries, headed for Velepromet. The other one's name was Pero Pavlica. There is another one that I remember who I believe to be very important. He was nicknamed Capalo. His real name is Mirko Vojnovic. While we were standing at the corridor, the gate itself and on the steps just outside the hospital, he entered the hospital, he cursed our Ustasha mother saying that he was on his way down to the basement where he would kill some Ustashas. We know this man, everybody knows him in Vukovar. He was a common criminal before the war. He never worked in order to earn his living. He lived by crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal with Capalo, the man you called Vojnovic. How was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: He was wearing a JNA uniform but it was a very jaded and threadbare one, quite dirty. I don't know how it got to be that way. It did look like a JNA uniform though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to say if he was armed whilst in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was armed. He was carrying an automatic rifle slung over his shoulder. I saw this when he passed me. I saw him carry a pistol too. I was just at the gate myself at this point in time and I saw him clearly as he was passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You mentioned initially a man called Jergic who you said wanted to kill you. How was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: He was wearing the same clothes as Capalo. And this other man I know, he is unfortunately dead. He died during his exile in the camp [as interpreted] later on. Gabrijel Mataija who was with him also said later that he had been wearing a JNA uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. I believe we have a slight problem with the transcript, page 30, line 12. It says [in English] "the camp." I believe this is not what the witness said. If my learned friend could please re-ask the question in order to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Have you followed that point, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: To be truthful, I haven't. The transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may help, this is page 30, line 12. It says -- lines 12 and 13. That is the sentence I'm talking about. I believe the witness actually said something else, and if my learned friend could please clarify this. It's about the death of this person that the witness has mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour give me a moment, please? Because it doesn't accord with my recollection. I want to clarify something. Well, I will try and clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Witness, one of the replies that you have given we are not sure whether it has been correctly recorded. You mentioned initially a man called Jergic who had said had wanted to kill you and you said that he was dressed in the same clothes as Capalo. And then you said there was another man I know who is unfortunately dead. Now, can you tell us how that person died?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Of course I can. I'm talking about Gabrijel Mataija. If I understand your question, he was in the Sremska Mitrovica camp and he had sustained severe injuries to his body. He spent a long time in a number of hospitals. He eventually died. I can't say when exactly, but soon after, I believe it was in 1993 that he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question, and then that would be the convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to ask you then, please, about when it was you came to leave the Vukovar Hospital. Now, when was that, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I left the Vukovar Hospital in the evening, or perhaps it was already night. But neither my wife nor I wore a watch, and I can only give you very rough assessment of what time it was. It might have been 9.00 or 10.00 that we were boarded onto this lorry and taken away. It was at this gate that I mentioned earlier that I clapped eyes on Pero Pavlica who was my neighbour's neighbour, and we are still neighbours, Milan Pavlica, the brother. He was just monitoring this process whereby people were being boarded on these lorries. Again, I say regardless of anything -- well, you see, this man too died two months ago, and regardless of everything that happened back then, seeing as his brother is a very good person, I'm still sorry that he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be a convenient moment, and we can then move on to this area of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. We will break now and assume at a quarter past 4.00. Oh, there was a redaction, it will be 20 past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I really do need a break. I would really appreciate it if it's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have that break now then, and we will resume at 20 past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, we had reached the situation where you were being loaded onto trucks. Who was in charge of the loading of the trucks?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: As for the loading of the trucks in order to drive people to Velepromet, the TO members, as they called themselves, were in charge of this. Prior to that we had seen an officer. He came, he gave an order, or maybe he didn't. He just came and left. The local TO people, as they called themselves, ordered us to get on the trucks, those of us who could. We tried to climb. It was very difficult to get on these trucks. The saddest thing was that elderly people, elderly men and women were being dumped onto these trucks as though they were sacks of potatoes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal with the officer? Can you tell us about the officer himself? Officer with whom?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: He was certainly a JNA officer. I know what that uniform is like. During my career, I was often called to go and serve with the reserve forces. I know what a JNA officer's uniform looks like. I was certain that this man was an officer. I had not yet been loaded onto a truck. I saw this happen from the steps outside the hospital. I saw him arrive and leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what was his rank, are you able to assist us with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: It was too far away for me to get a good look, and it was night-time. I couldn't see his rank, but I did see the cap and the uniform. Other people too told me that this was a JNA officer. Those people who saw him from close up at Velepromet later on. They said it was a JNA officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us about the elderly. Can you go into more detail about how the elderly were treated when they were being loaded on the trucks?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This military truck had no steps for lowering so that people could climb. Those who were young and still strong climbed by using their hands and arms. Elderly women were hardly able to walk, and then the TO men would raise them and simply chuck them onto the truck. It was a very sad thing to watch, very distressing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when a truck was full, what would then happen?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: When a truck was full, which meant that people were really, really pressed for space, it was really crowded, in a normal situation these trucks could hold as many as 25 people. In this case there were about 50 people on each of those. It was a very difficult situation, especially for the elderly who had been dumped onto these trucks. But, well, that's how it was. Eventually they drove us to Velepromet. Not straight away. First they took us across the street to the Vupik courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Before we reach the Vupik courtyard, can we deal with how packed the trucks were. How did that affect the elderly and infirm people?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: It was very difficult for the elderly and the infirm. We tried to help as best we could by supporting them or helping them sit down and then the rest of us would squeeze more closely. The only thing I can add to that is what I found personally very affecting. As we were being transported, we saw a number of dead bodies lying next to the road. And when we were crossing the Vuka I recognised a person by the upper part of his clothing. This was the working uniform of our company. And the person was an employee of the company by the name of Zvonimir Vilner. The path from the hospital to Vupik was the most difficult part for me personally. I thank you for letting me clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us about the person that you saw who had your company's uniform, as you described it. Do you know if he was involved in any military activity?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: The person who stood at the gates to the hospital, is that the person you have in mind? If you have him in mind, he was standing there. He wasn't participating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, you've told us that on the drive you saw a body of someone that you recognised from the upper part of his body. Do you remember your evidence on that? Now what I want you -- you know his name. Now, can you tell us, because you say you knew him, was he involved in any military activity throughout this conflict or in November?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: He was one of the defenders, as I learned later. I saw his jacket, which was a part of the working clothes in the company, we had that and we distributed it amongst the people. And I recognised the jacket and when I took a better look, I recognised Zvonimir Vilner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you have told us about the Vupik area. Now, whereabouts is the Vupik area?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: The road passes between Vupik and Velepromet. When one follows that direction, on the left-hand side there is the Vupik and right across the road is Velepromet. It used to be a large trading company. And they traded across the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal, please, then, with your arrival at the Vupik area? Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. When you arrived at the Vupik area, how many metres would it be from the Velepromet main gates?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: 30 metres at the most. The distance, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how far away from the Vupik area where you stopped would be the JNA barracks enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Approximately we passed by the barracks earlier, and it is also on the left-hand side of the road as well as Vupik. As to the distance between the barracks and Vupik, it may be around three to 400 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal, please, with the unloading of the lorries that had come from the hospital. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us then deal with that, please, if we may. How was the unloading done?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't by any violent means. They just ordered us to step down from the trucks. Those of us who could, we jumped out as fast as we could. And then we helped the elderly; we would support them and lower them to the ground. Unfortunately I must say that there were children among the people on the trucks as well and we helped them down as well. That's concerning the unloading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who was in charge of the unloading of the lorries?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: The TO people. They came to the trucks and they yelled at us that we need to come down from the trucks. And as I said, those of us who could climb down went first and then we helped the rest. And all of the civilians were more or less forming one group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you remain in one group?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: As soon as the unloading was finished and after we have helped the elderly and the infirm, we saw an officer who appeared there and he issued an order concerning separation. They started separating right away. They separated women and children and very old people on one side, and the defenders and the remainder of the civilians and men were on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us that you saw an officer. Are you able to say what rank or unit to which he belonged?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I am certain he was a JNA officer. I don't know the rank, and it was dark. It was difficult to see. I couldn't see whether he had two or three stars and was unable to determine his rank. I suppose he was either a lieutenant or captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us that there was a separation of women and children and defenders and men. If we just deal with the defenders and men, did they remain together as a group or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they stayed together in the group. After the officer left, we didn't hear any order being issued to the TO people, but they began separating right away and they separated approximately 50 people, one of whom was myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When we say 50 people, do we mean men or women or were they just -- was there just one sex chosen?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Only men. Women, children and the elderly had already been separated, taken towards the barracks. They were about 100 metres away by that time. We could see them standing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you recognise anyone within the TO who was dealing with you at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I recognised one person. His name is Darko Fot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: He only had the upper part of the TO uniform. The TO people seldom wore the entire uniform. They either had the pants or just the upper part of the uniform. He had the upper part. Since I knew him quite well since before the war, I recognised him immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did he say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Among the 50 people separated, he came to me, unfortunately, and he told me to follow him some five to six metres away from the group. He shouted insults and threats at me. He didn't injure me in any way, but he tried to intimidate me, and I can offer further explanation, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Was he armed at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was armed. He had an automatic rifle and when he asked me to say my name I was quite surprised. I told him, "Darko, why are you asking me that, since you know me very well?" He loaded his gun, it was a clear threat, and he told me to shout my name. I told him, "Yes, my name is Josip Covic, if you want to know," but he wasn't happy with that. He asked me to shout as loudly as I can, and he charged his gun, and that was a very clear threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When this was occurring, did you see how other people in the group were being treated?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I did. The rest of the group was standing there observing. No one was doing anything to them at that moment. They were just there listening to and observing the situation that was going on between me and Darko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did Darko Fot leave your group at any time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: If I may add something concerning Darko Fot and the way he treated me, after having asked me for my name he asked me what I had in my pockets. I said that I had some medication since a year before that I had had a lung operation in 1990. So I answered that I have some medication, that I am still taking it. He forced me to take it out of my pocket and discard it. That's what I needed -- I had to do. At that moment a JNA officer appeared, and I can proceed if you want me to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let us deal with the JNA officer arriving. What did he do?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: He appeared there some 10 metres away. We all heard him say that we should all be taken across the street to Velepromet. At that moment when he issued that order, or right after that, he left, and Darko Fot turned immediately to his TO men, saying we have to gather up in one place, and he pointed where, because there is another task for us at Ovcara. At that time I didn't know what the task could be. And they started crossing the road and the group crossed as well, including myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us then deal, please, with your transfer to the Velepromet facility. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us that there was a group of men that were chosen or isolated, perhaps a better way of putting it. What happened to that group of men that you were one of?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: That group that had been separated, including myself, after having crossed the road were told to line up in front of the hangar, and all the rest of the people entered the hangar. We spent -- the rest of the time before being loaded onto the trucks to the camps, we spent all that time standing in front of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you, for clarification, were you placed inside or outside a hangar at this time? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I remember it very well. I was in front of the hangar. As I was one of the people separated, we were lined up and the local civilians passed next to our group, pointing at certain people, and those people would then be taken behind the hangar, some 50 metres away, to Ciglana, and they were killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Before we get to that area, were you able to work out or assess who was in charge of the Velepromet facility at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: At that time the TO. We recognised most of them. They were doing the whole thing. The civilians were pointing people out and then they would call out Seselj's men to take those people behind the hangar towards Ciglana and then we could hear muffled shots. They may have used silencers as I learned later on to kill those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I deal with your position on the outside of the hangars? Did you have anyone guarding you at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: In the strict sense of the word, there was no one guarding, but there would appear every now and then the TO men. And they would take certain people away. But they didn't take away only some of the people from the group separated in front of the hangar, but as well from the hangar itself. On the opposing side there was an office and they kept taking two or three people there and most of them were later on taken to be killed. But -- and a small portion was returned to the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How do you know people were being killed as opposed to be just taken away?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I know that because I saw that. And Ivica Kopf, my sister's son, was taken away. I saw that as well. I felt terrible to see my nephew being taken away. And when we were being transported to the camps, all the people who used to work me and who went to the camps as well, they all told me, Josip, did you see that your Ivica was taken away and was killed? And my response was yes, I did see that, and it was a very difficult thing for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you able to recognise any of the TO members at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see that the dead body since that was some 50 metres behind the hangar; we were not there. Later on in the camp, I can explain, although my nephew was taken there he wasn't killed in the end and he himself told me what happened. As he was about to get killed, a colleague, schoolmate of his from the TO appeared, they shared the same bench, and this man took him away. He said, "Don't kill him, he is my schoolmate." He later appeared at the camp where I was, and I was reborn to see my nephew alive. He told me how the killings took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's clearly my fault. The question I think that I asked you was the TO who were controlling you at the camp, I asked you whether -- let me just finish, if I may. Did you recognise any of those TO members? Can you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all right. I misunderstood, my apologies. I did recognise some. For example, Mile Macesic. He was from the same part of the city as I was, a few houses away. He went to school with my son. He wanted to kill me. Before that there was a crime that took place. One of the civilians pointed out a young man. He said that his name was Kemo. I'm not absolutely certain, but it was a nickname of sorts. And he called two Chetniks to come. They came and they slit his throat in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just ask you to stop, please? Because I want to go back and we'll deal with Kemo in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies for interrupting, Your Honours. I just wanted to point out to something I don't know whether I am correct, but I can see some notes before the witness. I don't know whether he refers to the notes, and I don't know whether it can be tolerated for him to use them. I would kindly ask for some instruction from the Bench, because I don't know what the situation actually is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, could you explore the situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, of course I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, can you be -- it's been suggested you have some notes in front of you. Is that right or not? On your desk.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I will gladly explain. It's been over 14 years since Vukovar fell and all the crimes there took place. For any person it would be difficult to remember all the names, and what I have here on this piece of paper are the names of the people I saw at Velepromet and in the hospital. I don't know whether this is permitted, but I will gladly remove it, although I wouldn't be quite able to comprehend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you could please put that aside, the list of names, and just try and remember as best you can as Mr. Moore asks questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just see the note, as I've never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly. Please. Feel free. Actually, I prefer that you have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic may wish to see it as well. Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really made an assumption based on what I have seen. I do not wish to create a problem, but I think it's very much up to the President as regards what the witness is doing right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will continue without the list. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, just to refocus on the group of men who you say had been chosen and then placed outside the hangars? Now, you told us that there were approximately 50 men and that through that period some were being taken away. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The question I want to ask you is this: Out of the 50 how many were actually taken away?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Out of those 50 men who were in that column, by the time we started towards the trucks and were about to be taken to the camp, there were only about a half of the people who had originally been there, which means that over a half had been taken away to be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can I ask you then this question: Of the 25 that were taken away, how many of those did you ever see again?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't able to see any of them. I only saw them being taken away, first behind the hangar and then in the direction of the brick factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Sorry, perhaps it's the way I put the question. I'll ask it again. You have 25 people taken away. You have told us that your nephew eventually you were aware did come back. Did you see any of the others come back or see any of the others at the camp or indeed afterwards? Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. No, I never saw any of them. My nephew was not among those 50 men. He was in the hangar and that's where he was taken away from. That section of the hangar was facing the other way, so he passed in front of us, passed the hangar and on to the brick factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again, some may want to know what happened to the 25 people who were taken away? Do you know either from your own knowledge or what you were told?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I am certain about this. Both in the camp and after, once we had left the camp, there were people who told me that the killing had gone on throughout the night by the brick factory. There are people who claim, and I am one of these, that at least twice as many people had been killed at Velepromet than at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When these people were taken away, you have referred to the use, as you have stated, a silencer being used. When these people were taken away, did you at any time hear gun-fire coming from the area where they were taken to?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear gun-fire. This gun-fire continued throughout practically,, there were lulls that would last two or three minutes and then the firing would start again. It was like this throughout, at least for as long as I was still at Velepromet. As for the rest, we know that in addition to them being taken to the camp, some people had stayed behind at Velepromet, which was turned into some sort of a camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to now deal with evidence that you gave where you referred to a person called Kemo. Do you remember the evidence that you gave?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I told this person called Kemo that a civilian had come by. I recognised three civilians. There was one civilian who pointed out that particular young man and this one I didn't know. It was a lady who pointed him out. At this point a TO man came along, came up to this young man and he called over two Chetniks, two of Seselj's men who were wearing the full Chetnik attire. They had cockades on their fur caps. One of them wore the military kind and sported a long beard. There was a bottle containing some sort of a drink sticking out of his pocket. He had knives on him, too, as well as an automatic rifle. They slit this young man's throat right there in front of us, gave him short shrift. The young man just lay there for about 15 minutes at least in a pool of his own blood, after which his body was dragged away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How close were you to this young man Kemo having his throat cut?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: To my great sadness, this happened not more than three metres away from where I was standing. A Chetnik grabbed him by the upper arms and held him tight while the other plunged a knife into his throat all the way through. They just dropped his body on the ground. I saw him twitch once or twice, and then he was dead. There was a huge pool of blood forming underneath his body and he was probably dead by this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you see any soldier, any TO make any attempt to stop what was going on that night at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence -- just a minute, please, sir. I have an objection. I believe my learned friend should first ask the following questions: Were there any JNA officers around; and then the next question should be did any of them take any steps to prevent this. I believe this to be a leading question as it stands now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it's quite valid, Mr. Moore, that your question assumes the presence of certain people at relevant times to this conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Then I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you saw this man having his throat cut, did you see anyone try to stop this action?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: No. No one at all came to stop this. The next person to arrive was Mile Macesic. He pointed out to me and tried to have the Chetniks do the same thing to me as they had done to this young man. If need be, I can tell you what happened to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, who was Mile Macesic? Can you tell the Court?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Mile Macesic was from my neighbourhood, three houses down the street. He was even my son's classmate. When he arrived and spotted me he yelled out, "There's your old Ustasha. He has a son. His son is a hard core Ustasha. His name is Drazen. He used to be president of the HDZ youth club." Which simply wasn't true because my son never was, not even before the war. Those two Chetniks who were some distance away from us, by this time he sent one of them back and said, "There you go, take care of this one, too, for me, will you. And he came up to me and started punching me. At this point, to my great fortune, another JNA officer emerged from somewhere, called those two over and ordered them to join him in order to go and do a job. As they were leaving they said, "We'll be back and we'll make sure to settle our accounts with you." I'm not sure if that answers your question. If not, please, feel free to request further clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will ask for some further clarification. You have told us that you were punched and beaten by these two men who had murdered Kemo. Do you remember that? And you have described a JNA officer arriving and speaking to them. Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think I said he was talking to them. He just called them over and ordered them to come with him. Because there was a job that needed doing. That -- those were his precise words. I'm not sure what the job was that he was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When he called them over, what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: They immediately followed. But once they were about to leave one of them turned around to face me and say, "We will be back to settle our accounts with you."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Please listen to this question carefully. When the JNA officer spoke to them or called across to them, what were they doing? Not what they did. What were they doing.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: When he called them they started towards me. I stepped back slightly and then they started punching me with their fists. I received two or three blows like that. I had already made up my mind that I will not allow them to slit my throat, that I would do anything, that I would kick and scream and even ask them to put a bullet through my head, just in order not to have my throat slit. To my great fortune, a JNA officer appeared as I set to call them about a job that needed doing. It's pure fate, you might say. And this lucky circumstance saved my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So I ask the question again. When the JNA officer called them what were these two TO soldiers doing at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, sir, please. First of all, the transcript, page 48, line 16. It says two TO soldiers, we're not talking about TO soldiers, we're talking about Chetniks here. That's the first thing. The other thing, I believe the witness has now for two or three times provided the same identical answer to this question and this is third time it's been asked. I think the witness is being led in some way in order to change his testimony. The previous answer on the same page provides an excellent explanation of what these two men were doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the comment about TO is right, Mr. Moore. The -- I can't see that there is any leading as implied, but haven't you got an answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, in my submission the answer -- yes, inferentially, of course, I have got the answer, but the question is quite specific, and in my submission the witness is not fully understanding the nature of the question, because the reply is -- does not correspond with the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it corresponds but adds more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't really know, all I -- may I ask the question one more time to see -- I think there may be a translation problem or the witness does not fully understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't see it, but go ahead and one more shot and then Mr. Vasic is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, you have told us that you were being beaten and that a JNA officer arrived and called to these two men. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: At the actual time that he called these two men, what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: They were about to leave. They were leaving when this officer called them. I believe that the question is phrased quite fairly; however, I do not agree with the objection. Those were clever questions, and all I did was tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'll move on, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When these two Chetniks said that they would be back, how close was the JNA officer to them when they said that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I suppose the distance might have been about 10 metres. Not more or less. He didn't walk right up to them at all. He just called to them, telling them -- telling them there was a job to be done. And they left immediately. As they were leaving, one of them turned back to threaten me, same as my previous answer. I'm happy with your question. And all I'm trying is to tell the truth and nothing but the truth. If there is anything that doesn't quite sound right, I will certainly say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When the Chetnik called out that he would deal with you afterwards, where were you actually located at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: At that time I was still standing outside the hangar, same spot as before. All I can do is thank my fate. Before long another officer arrived from somewhere else. I could clearly see that this was a major. He ordered for us to get onto the trucks that eventually took us to the camps. I was lucky to survive, you might say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And a major with whom, are you able to say?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: A JNA major. I clearly saw this from close up. He walked up to us and he gave instructions on how we should proceed, that we should walk in twos, that we should hold each other's hands. People were already leaving the hangar and we did exactly as he had instructed us and we headed for the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So can you tell us now, please, about being loaded onto the buses? When did that happen shall please?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: This happened later on during the night. I think it might have been about 5.00 a.m. This was all happening in November, so it was still quite dark. It might have been at 4.00 or 5.00 a.m., but it was still dark by the time we started getting onto the buses. My apologies, I said trucks but I meant buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: They drove us to Sremska Mitrovica where they parked all the buses. Not inside the camp itself but right outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who was in charge of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: On the buses, on each of the buses there were two JNA soldiers. Judging by the way they looked, their physical appearance, they were young, young men, aged 20-ish, doing their regular military service in all likelihood. Those soldiers were standing next to the driver at the front of the bus. All I can say is that they didn't beat anyone and more power to them. They were upright lads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There is one question that I should have asked you, and I apologise to you for omitting it. You have told us about people being taken away from outside the hangar, 25 out of 50. Did you see anybody else being taken away from any other part of the Velepromet facility?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. There was plenty on the other side too. We didn't see that because there is an enormous building running down the middle. This was the administration building inside the Velepromet compound. There were plenty of civilians on the other side too. As they were leading them away they had to pass that building, us, and the hangar, so we saw them being led to the brick factory. We saw those people being led to the brick factory to be killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to say how many times or how many people you saw being led away to the -- to the brick factory?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: This went on the whole time. It's difficult for me to say. I learned later about those who were -- had remained in the hangars as prisoners. I reckon, as I have already said, I think twice as many men were killed at Velepromet as at Ovcara, unfortunately, it has to be said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who was taking them across to the brick factory to be killed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: They were being taken across by Seselj's men, by Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I know how difficult it is to estimate time, over what period of time were people being taken away, either from the hangar or from the other areas to be killed? Are you able to assess over what period of time that was?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: This went on the whole night and then I was loaded onto a bus along with the all the others. Throughout this time people were being led away. Those who stayed behind confirmed this to me. The killing had gone on for the whole night. It's very difficult to say anything about the exact figures. However, later on, once we had learned how many people had been killed and when the mass graves were dug up, we just knew that many, many more people had been killed at Velepromet than at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you at any time hear of the Chetniks being stopped from killing these people or any attempt to stop the killing of these people throughout this period?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: No, never. I never heard of any attempts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour consider that perhaps an appropriate moment for this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Moore. We'll have a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think it is about that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I would really like a break. I would love a break. I was just about to ask. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I thank Your Honours. Might I just indicate to my learned friends that -- and to the Court that I have spoken to my learned friends about the final part of this witness's evidence, which relates his transportation back and his stay in the camps and I am allowed -- permitted to lead in relation to that, so I think it's called official leading as opposed to unofficial leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber might have a different description of this, Mr. Moore, but please go ahead and I thank counsel for the Defence. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, can we just deal, then, please, with your transfer from Velepromet to Sremska Mitrovica? I think it's right to say that you were taken on buses. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. On buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And those buses were escorted by JNA soldiers. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: It is correct. Those were young JNA soldiers, and I thought they were actually serving their military term with the JNA at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Might I ask you in non-leading form the following question: How were you treated on the way, on the way to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: They treated us fairly, and I was satisfied. They told us how and where to sit and to abide by what they tell us. They didn't beat anyone or anything else. I am quite happy with their conduct and with the way they carried out that task, received by their superiors, no doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how did the local people treat you or deal with you as you went through various areas?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: We didn't stop on the way. When we stopped it was in front of the camp in Mitrovica. An officer came into the bus and he went from one bus to another and when he came to our bus he ordered us not to leave the bus, and he must have done the same thing with the other buses. And when we had to go to the toilet we couldn't leave, but we had to do it on the bus. That was particularly difficult. The soldiers who were in our escort, they remained and the local population that passed by the buses was hitting on the windows and threatening. On the bus where I was two men climbed up and slapped a few people, but the two soldiers forced them out and didn't let them return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what were the local people threatening to do?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: They were cursing, telling that we should all be killed, they were calling us names, Ustashas, threatening in general. And I remember it quite well that the two soldiers took those two men out who were slapping the people seated in the front seats. And I felt quite safe for as long as they were not allowed to come on board and they can threaten all they want.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to deal with your arrival at a camp which is situated close to the Romanian border. I think it is pronounced Stajicevo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Stajicevo, yes. You pronounced it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, when you arrived, what -- what was the procedure at the very outset to enter the camp?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: The procedure was such that they told us to come off the buses. The people waiting there were not soldiers. We thought they were all Chetniks. They were issuing orders. We saw at least a hundred of them standing in two columns. We were told to walk in between the columns towards the camp. And where they kept us in the camp, that was the stable for cattle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you tell us the sort of beatings that you personally underwent, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Since we had to pass between them, and there must have been a hundred of them, 50 on each side, and they all had something in their hands, they were beating us. Those who managed to get through were yelling back at us don't go down by any means because if you do, they start kicking you. And I managed somehow, having received some strikes to reach the entrance to the camp.
