And perhaps I can reply to a question that I believe will come somewhat later, but there were people who were badly injured during the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I just want to deal with yourself, if I may, at this time. You told us that you had your -- your jaw broken. How did that occur?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: When I went to the toilet once -- but, rather, it wasn't a toilet but an area dedicated for that purpose just outside the stable, and every time we would return there were five or six men at the entrance and one had to pass by them or between them. As I was returning they started hitting me. I fell on the ground, and since they were wearing boots they kept kicking. They were kicking on my head and they broke my jaw, my teeth, my nose was crushed. And when they finally stopped I managed to drag myself back inside. There was a veterinarian with me in the camp, and he took a look at my face. He said, "Don't worry, there are a few things broken. Just keep spitting all the blood that comes into your mouth," and I kept doing so for three days. And that was several days before the exchange. That's when I left the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you ever interrogated in this camp?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I was interrogated twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And during the interrogation did you receive any beatings?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: During the interrogations, yes, I was beaten once. The other time they didn't beat me. The interrogations were conducted by JNA officers, and I told that particular JNA officer on that occasion that I was very sad to have lived through this, that I have a colleague, a friend by the name of Cuk who was a colonel. This officer took that name down, he probably ran a check, and after that interrogation the officer called me out of the room where the interrogation took place. He ordered the Seselj's men in my escort not to beat me and that I should be allowed to sit and have a rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were any allegations made against you personally by that interrogating officer?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Those particular officers did not make any allegations. However, I told them that I used to be a reserve officer and I served rather often with the reserve forces, and I received a rank. Hence they thought I was a direct participant of the events, but I tried to explain that I was only offering advice to our defendants, how to protect their lives and to avoid being killed or injured during combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What sort of premises were you confined in at this particular camp?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: It was a huge stable for cattle. It had a concrete floor and we had to lie on that floor, and the temperature at the time was minus 10 or minus 15 degrees centigrade. After a few days, we received some hay to put on the floor. And a lot of people became ill before the camp was closed, because of the low temperatures. Pneumonia was a regular occurrence; I suffered from it myself. And people would have died in greater numbers had it not been for the closure of the camp after 33 days and some exchanges took place. The rest were transferred to Mitrovica, Nis and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You told us that you had concussions to your head which was affected your memory. How did that occur?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: As I explained before, I was beaten and I described the nature of my injuries. Having returned from the camp my head was X-rayed, and during the treatment the doctors told me that I had sustained an injury to a particular part of the brain which stores memory. I used to know a lot of songs, and I liked singing, but I complained that I can't remember a single verse. And they explained to me that the memory part of the brain was damaged and that the beating was the cause and that there wasn't much they could do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us about the attacks upon yourself during an interrogation and other times. Did you see other people being treated in an aggressive way when you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. A part of the stable was -- they left a square or four by four metres in the stable and they beat some young people in that spot until they killed them. Of those people, two I knew from before, one was Ivica Kemal [phoen] and the other one was Koh. That was his last name. I can't remember his first name but he used to work construction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How did they kill them?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to this line of questioning. As far as I understood, at a given point a question was to be put to the witness about Stajicevo and the stable, but it seems to me that we are now going into details which are outside the framework of the indictment in terms of time and space. I don't know whether we need to listen to all of this since the indictment concerns itself with different events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I accept entirely it's outside the framework of the indictment. I understand that, and it will never be advanced to that end. But this witness has said that he has suffered from post-traumatic stress. The Court have got to assess his credibility. They've got to assess what it is that he underwent. If it was merely a case of the evidence in relation to what I would call Vukovar, then that would give a false picture. In my submission, I am trying to deal with it as succinctly as I can. It gives a totality of the experience that he had and allows the Court - and I hope my learned friends - to assess whether in actual fact the evidence that he gave was affected by or is affected by the events that he has described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Moore, keeping it to that very brief basis that you have indicated and for the purposes that have been indicated, and not relevant to the question of guilt or innocence of any of the particular counts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I accept that fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you tell us then, please, how they were killed? You said you saw young men being killed.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw them beat on the two men I knew. They used various objects to beat them until they fell to the ground. Once down they kept kicking them with their boots, they jumped on their chest, hitting their heads for as long as they showed any signs of life. The one I mentioned, Ivica Kamel, I used to know him quite well. He was a young man, married, quite tall, good-looking. As we were getting out of the stable and when we passed by his body, I couldn't recognise any of the features of his head. You couldn't see where the nose or the eye or the lips were. It was just a mass. It looked -- his head resembled a ball. That's what sort of death he met. And that's the truth and I can remember it quite vividly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what affect did that have upon you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: It had a deep impact on me. And when I underwent treatment in 1992 a doctor by the name of Kondrozo [phoen] told me that the injuries that I sustained could be cured but after five years I will still have severe psychological trauma based on what I saw, because it is then that the post-traumatic stress disorder symptoms will occur and they didn't know the exact treatment for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic will now ask you some further questions. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let him ask by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, Mr. Domazet will take that role on behalf of the Defence, but if he could have a minute to get ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have got him into some view now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Mr. Covic. My name is Vladimir Domazet, counsel for Mr. Mrksic. I wanted to ask you some questions, and I would kindly ask you to answer to those questions, but do bear in mind that we should make pause between question and answer for the sake of interpreters and court reporters. Today in your statement when you mentioned your data, personal data, one could see that you spent most of your lifetime in Vukovar itself. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. After having finished my education, the rest of my life was in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You were born close to Vukovar, not in Vukovar itself?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was born in Bogdanovci, which is the closest village to Vukovar. After having finished my high school education I moved to Vukovar where I stayed for the rest of my life, apart from the 10 years after the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, since we are discussing your education, you said that you completed your high school outside of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: No, in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you hold any higher degree?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I completed college for economic affairs, which is a two-year type education. I didn't manage to get to the bachelor's degree, since I was under a lot of stress and work in the company itself, and the company didn't need me to have a bachelor's degree, hence I never completed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understood properly, you worked as someone who held a -- had a high school diploma and you attended the college at the same time when you started working. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The part of the city including your house, is that close to Sajmiste, the part that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Sajmiste is probably 1500 metres away. But looking from our part towards Bogdanovci on the outskirts of the city up to Mitnica, that part was called Sajmiste, the defence line. But the very Sajmiste Street, that runs from the barracks towards the city. And the entire defence line was named after the street, Sajmiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your answer was quite long. Could we try to clear up a few things? Did I understand correctly that your house is relatively close to Sajmiste, or rather close to the front line?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is close to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, to go back to a period before that, and could you please answer a couple of questions concerning Vukovar before the outbreak of the war? To my colleague's question today you replied that you were politically active, that you were a member of the League of Communists up until the war. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you tell me what were relations between the ethnic groups in Vukovar and its environs before the first multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Even before the multi-party elections the relations were no longer good. Most people in Croatia, after the speeches given by your Milosevic -- well, not your, but the Milosevic of the Serbs, and one would clearly see the threats stemming from his speeches, and we were expecting an evil to occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, you are referring to the period before the multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I may phrase it that way, there was a sort of mistrust between the two ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We sensed this threat from the famous speeches by Milosevic. And we knew that something would take place later. That he had something in store. The Slovenians were the first to react to his speeches and then of course the people from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It's not my intention to dwell on this, but one thing I would like to ask you is: Slobodan Milosevic, the man you were talking about, was also a member of the League of Communists, the only party in Yugoslavia at the time, was it not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell me what happened after the first multi-party elections? In Croatia itself it was the HDZ that garnered the majority, did it not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the HDZ won. After this we expected that the same thing would happen in the former Yugoslavia as it happened between the Slovakia and the Czech Republic. We expected civilised negotiations leading to the creation of separate states, as we see today. Or the same thing that had happened in the former Soviet Union. This unfortunately was not the case. I am greatly saddened by the fact that the matter could not have been resolved in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Fair enough. I believe you have strayed quite far from my question. I would like you to please stay true to the gist of my question. I want to ask you about the result of the elections, the outcome in Vukovar itself, especially the local elections.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Everything was perfectly normal and perfectly fine. However, even at this early stage, Vukovar Serbs would send their wives and children across the border to Backa or drive them there. I even asked some of our people at the company why are you sending your families away, can you please share that with us. If there is an impending danger, perhaps we should send our families too. They refused to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You still haven't answered my question, Mr. Covic. Can you please try and have another go. What was the outcome of the local elections in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: The greatest number of votes was garnered by the HDZ. The other parties were all minor parties. Despite this, everything was perfectly normal -- or, rather, specifically in Vukovar it wasn't the HDZ. I really apologise. It was the SDP carried the day in Vukovar at the local elections. And we were quite happy to see that happen. That was what the people decided. That was what the voters' body decided. That was all. There were no further problems. I do have to say, however, that the Serbs had already begun to send their families away from Vukovar. We found this strange, and we asked them about their reasons why were they doing this despite the fact that the elections had been perfectly smooth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Again, I have you answering something that you weren't asked in the first place. But now that you've said this, what about the fear these people felt? Was this a fear grounded in reality? These people were after all sending their families away. One probably wouldn't do this sort of thing unless you had a real concern about their safety?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: That may be your opinion, but it certainly isn't mine. As soon as they refused to tell us, my own work-mates, for example, we had been working together for 20 years, and you have this person refusing to talk about their reasons. And probably these people were in the loop. They knew why they were doing this and they knew exactly why they kept refusing to share this with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, it's all right. I will try to go back to my previous line of questions. Please bear with me, I do have several other questions on this same subject. Who was the first elected president of municipality of these first local elections in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to tell you this: It is as a result of my injury, the injuries to the memory cells in my brain, all I can say is that he was a Serb who hailed from Trpinje residing, however, in Vukovar, and he was the president of town. You must know this too, I believe this individual was tried at this Tribunal and he eventually committed suicide.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously you remember that the gentleman's name was Slavko Dokmanovic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. Thank you for reminding me. As I say, it's a problem that I have because of my brain injury. Sometimes I find it difficult to remember names. Names just tend to escape me. But, yes, indeed, that's true, Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, do you remember how long he remained in that position and who he was replaced by?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: He remained in this position for a certain time. I can't say exactly. When the incident occurred at Borovo Selo and when Seselj's men and Chetniks began to arrive, our electricians at company told me personally as early as -- in March or April 1991 they had passed through Borovo Selo to fix some electricity cables. And they told me, "Oh, we've seen some Chetniks over in Borovo Selo." I didn't believe it at the time, although they even went as far as saying, "Come on join us, get in the car with us, we can just drive through and you can see for yourself." But then he stepped down and he went somewhere else. Left Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can I take that to mean that the Dokmanovic ceased to be president of Vukovar municipality after the incident in Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May, 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I can't say that coincides with this date or not. But it was roughly at this time, give or take a month or two. I can't say exactly. I can give you very rough idea of what I remember. He was just gone. And then another person came who occupied this post on a provisional basis, a local.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was it possible by this time to have communication between all these different places, Trpinje, the place where Mr. Dokmanovic hailed from. Could you reach Vukovar from Trpinje smoothly with no problems at all?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: After the serious crime that occurred at Borovo Selo when 22 police officers were killed, in the predominantly Serb villages around Vukovar, those that had a Serb majority, barricades were set up and it was very difficult to drive through these places or to reach Vukovar from Osijek, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were there barricades before the 2nd of May, 1991, before Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: No. It wasn't until after the incident that all these barricades sprang up in Brsadin, in Trpinje, in Negoslavci and all those other places. There was even a Serb from Brsadin who was a proper man, an upright man. , and he still is. This man used to come over. It was very difficult to obtain permission to go to work in Vukovar from Brsadin. He was greatly aggrieved by this and he asked for our help so that we might help him to continue to go to work. He still complained about the difficulties that he faced on his way to Vukovar. He was an ethnic Serb but he was an upright, honest person. And he still is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Although he was an ethnic Serb, he was an upright person. I'm glad to know that. But I want to know about these barricades. Were Croats perhaps erecting barricades too? Perhaps that's why he as a Serb had trouble passing through.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: There were a few Croats to begin with over in Brsadin. I don't think they would have been in a position to erect any barricades. It was a predominantly Serb village, and it was the Serbs who erected those barricades, and they chose who they would let through.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I didn't mean Brsadin specifically when I spoke about the barricades, him being a local and all that. But what about Borovo Naselje, for example? You will agree with me that it had a Croat majority. Were there any barricades? Could he just drive through Borovo Naselje since there were barricades there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: No. He was perfectly free to drive straight through Borovo Naselje and get on with it. In Borovo Naselje and in Borovo Selo, right after the incident, it was no longer possible to pass through. But he did not have any difficulty going from Brsadin. He told us that he had been verbally abused severely for continuing to go to work in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the following cafes in Borovo Naselje: Slon and Zurich?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't go to restaurants much really. I'm not much of a restaurant-goer. It's always been like that. Not that I'm boasting or anything, but it just wasn't a habit that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm asking you because we have information to indicate that this was precisely where the barricades were that the residents of Borovo Naselje had erected. I was saying that in order to perhaps refresh your memory. But if not, not. I won't be pressing the point any further. What about the time that preceded Borovo Selo? Do you perhaps know that in predominantly Croatian villages or Croatian only villages unarmed units were being set up and assembled that Croatian politicians had a hand in this? Did you learn anything about that at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: The only thing I learned was about my own village Bogdanovci, but not about any other villages. I knew about Bogdanovci because my folks had told me. At this time, and I'm not sure about the date, it certainly wasn't long after the crime in Borovo Selo. One day a column of tanks arrived from Bogdanovci and wanted to drive straight through and onto Vukovar. But the entire population rose in a bid to stop the tanks from passing through the village. They were unarmed, barehanded. They just lay across the road, most of them did, and said, "There you go, over our dead bodies, if you have to." That is how they stopped this entire column of tanks that was on its way to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know who Tomislav Mercep was?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Mercep, yes, I do. He had been appointed this military sort of thing, I'm not sure what it's called. It used to be called different before. I really can't remember. But this is another consequence of my brain injury. He was appointed to some post or other on behalf of this military office that was in charge of recruiting young men to go to the army. I'm sure you know the proper name for this office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But he hailed from Bogdanovci, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Not from Bogdanovci. It wasn't until several years before the war when he started building a house in Bogdanovci. But he resided in Borovo Naselje and that's where he worked. It was just that several years before the war he and two of his brothers bought some land and built houses there. They lived there for a brief period of time, perhaps as long as a year or two. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I think you described this accurately. It was some sort of chief or head of this military recruitment office, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the recruitment office, I think that would be the exact name, the exact term. That's where he was appointed. He was appointed as chief or head.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: After relations began to cool and the first incidents occurred, was his role changed and was he not appointed to a rather more important position inside of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he had a prominent position in the party. He was the president of the local HDZ branch, so this was his other role, in a manner of speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know that it was he of all people who organised a review of the forces in Bogdanovci, one that was sponsored by the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I do know that he had a lot of people assembled there, and I know he introduced himself to them and he said that after Borovo Selo and in view of all the barricades, worse things were certain to happen. He called on the young to be ready in the eventuality of an attack against Vukovar. He said Vukovar should be ready to defend itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was a proper military review carried out on that occasion? With units and people in charge of these units, whatever they were called, because they were still unarmed at the time, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were all unarmed. And I don't think any commanders had been appointed by this time. He just called these people to assemble so that he could warn them about possible attacks, and he said that if any attacks should take place they should all stand up and defend their town. Many of the boys who were there told me about the reasons for them assembling there, and the gist of this meeting was if Vukovar was to be attacked, everybody would be prepared to defend it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you perhaps learn from them or from a different source what would be used in defence of the town? Is it not true that the purchase of weapons started, Kalashnikovs, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And unfortunately these were the days when the first purchases were made. I saw this for myself. Unfortunately, about 90 per cent of the total of the weapons they had was made up by hunting rifles. You could hardly see anybody carrying a proper rifle, an M-48 or something like that. It was a great surprise whenever I saw someone carrying a proper Kalashnikov. It was very rare. Once Vukovar had been attacked there were more of those kinds of weapons gradually and more and more weapons came in, and this is the only reason they managed to defend Vukovar for so long.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But I'm talking about the period preceding the outbreak of the war, I'm talking about the military reviews, I'm talking about armament. I'm asking if you know whether any weapons had been obtained unlawfully. You will agree with me that it was not a lawful thing to purchase a Kalashnikov then or now?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: There is one thing I have to tell you. It's the truth and nothing but the truth. I'm not sure if you're familiar with this. You might find this surprising. A large number of Kalashnikovs was purchased by our people from the Serbs. I know this. I couldn't help but laugh when I found out that some of the Serbs were selling weapons to us of all people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you for this piece of information. It's difficult to surprise me, but this really is a surprise because I didn't know about this. So this was yet another way of purchasing weapons at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was one of the channels used. If I may be allowed to ask a question, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Not to me. To the Chamber, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: It's to the Chamber. Are we having a break any time soon? Or are we just pressing straight through? If we could have another short break, that would be much appreciated, Your Honour. But if we only have a short time to go on, perhaps we should just continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We would normally finish in about eight minutes time from now, but if you feel uncomfortable, we'll finish now. Which would you prefer? Are you able to carry on for eight minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Certainly, Your Honour. Eight minutes shouldn't be a problem. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said several times that you were a reserve officer with the JNA. My question is: Which school for reserve officers did you complete and when?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: The one in Zadar back in 1961. That was tantamount to my military term, military service, the regular one. I was, I just have to say this, I was sent there to that school because I excelled as a student at my own school. I later spent six months in Zadar at the military school. I was one of the best students in terms of my grade-point average, so I was sent to serve with Tito's guards for another six months. So that was my military service, the long and short of it. Later on when I was already employed, they would call me at least two or three times a year to join the reserve forces, which caused a certain amount of grief back in my company. But I had to go, I had no choice. I was promoted several times over the years, eventually reaching the rank of captain first class. That was back in 1968 that I was awarded the rank following the attack on Czechoslovakia when the general concern was that Yugoslavia would be attacked by the Russians. It was then that I was appointed as a commander of the artillery company along the border with Hungary. So that was a success for me. I was awarded a relatively high rank, but this was nothing but a source of trouble back at work. That would be my answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you said you were sent to this reserve officer school because you were a good student at the time, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I hope you can answer this one. What about your membership in the League of Communists. Don't you think this had anything to do with your scholarship and being sent to the reserve officers' school?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: No, that had nothing to do with that. In our class back at school there were about 30 or 40 persons. They said right at the start the two with the best grades, once school was over, would be sent to Tito's personal guard, as some sort of a reward, and I came in at number two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Are you talking about the reserve officers' school or prior to that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the reserve officers' school, that's what I'm telling you about, the one back in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But I'm talking about being sent there to that school in the first place. Don't you think your party membership favoured you being sent there? Was this a perk or a privilege that you enjoyed at the time? In view of the fact that you had only completed your secondary education, was this the reason that you only stayed in the army for 12 months, otherwise regular military service would have been 18 months?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, that was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: We have several minutes left, and I would like to use this time to ask you a number of questions about Vukovar and what went on just before the clashes started. Do you know anything about explosions, fires shopping and newsstands being blown up?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear about that. There were several newsstands, and restaurants too, pubs. What I couldn't understand was why this always seemed to happen when there was nobody around, at daybreak. I felt that somebody was putting on a show in order to lead someone else down the garden path, but that's just my take on it. Obviously there were explosions in restaurants and pubs, but fortunately not a single person was wounded or killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can I take your answer to mean that you personally harboured certain suspicions about the owners themselves perhaps setting fires to their own establishments?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the owner themselves. There was one at Bogdanovacka Street. It was called Gornje Brdo [phoen]. The owner was someone who was later with the so-called TO attacking Vukovar. There was several explosions in his establishment, which was a tavern. No one was ever hurt. The next day he would fix it a little. He would stay open for a week, and then there would soon be another explosion, that sort of thing. Thank God no one got hurt. I had suspicions about this. No one was getting hurt. I suppose that he was staging these explosions and fires.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly that this owner as well as all the other owners who had this happening to their establishments was a Serb, an ethnic Serb?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were Serbs. Those that I know of. I can't speak about everybody. Vukovar is not such a small town after all, but things were happening. And I was at home, I was busy at work. I didn't have time to just walk around in order to find out what was happening. I only knew about those that were near me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just another question for today, and then I'm winding up. What about the Borba newsstand? Borba is a newspaper based in Belgrade, as you probably know. Was there any explosion? Was this kiosk blown up too?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that one, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe this is a good time to wrap it up for the day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so too. I absolutely agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. We will adjourn this evening and resume tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st day of February, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
